articles.title: Imbalanced Gray‐Green Infrastructure Closely Parallels Extreme Rainfall‐Flood Resilience Inequality Between Mainstream and Tributary Cities in the Pearl River Basin, Southern China
articles.titleEn: Imbalanced Gray‐Green Infrastructure Closely Parallels Extreme Rainfall‐Flood Resilience Inequality Between Mainstream and Tributary Cities in the Pearl River Basin, Southern China
articles.abstract: Climate change and rapid urbanization are intensifying flood risks, making unequal gray‐green infrastructure (GGI) provision a growing concern for extreme rainfall‐flood resilience (ERFR). However, how GGI inequality corresponds with ERFR differences between mainstream and tributary cities remains insufficiently understood. Using the 2025 Typhoon Wutip period as a fixed regional extreme‐event observation window, this study quantified GGI inequality and examined basin‐scale ERFR differentiation in southern China's Pearl River Basin (PRB). Representing GGI through drainage networks and aggregate urban green‐space provision, we combined the Gini coefficient with a machine‐learning‐based “flood sensitivity‐infrastructure vulnerability” framework to map basin‐wide ERFR and examine GGI‐ERFR relationships among 23 representative cities across hydrological and developmental contexts. Results revealed pronounced inequality in GGI provision. Mainstream cities generally exhibited higher green‐space ratios and drainage‐network densities, whereas tributary cities had more limited built‐up area‐based infrastructure provision. Correspondingly, ERFR exhibited marked spatial differentiation, with higher values concentrated in urban clusters, including the Pearl River Delta, and lower values more widely distributed across inland mountainous tributary areas. Built‐up area‐based GGI indicators showed the most pronounced inequality () and were strongly associated with ERFR (; ). Together, GGI concentration corresponded closely with the spatially heterogeneous distribution of ERFR across mainstream and tributary settings. These findings highlight the importance of directing infrastructure investment toward under‐resourced tributary areas and provide insights for hydrologically differentiated resilience governance in rapidly urbanizing river basins.

articles.title: Climate Change Forces Hydrological Regime Shifts in Australian Wetlands
articles.titleEn: Climate Change Forces Hydrological Regime Shifts in Australian Wetlands
articles.abstract: Wetlands provide crucial biodiversity benefits and ecosystem services but are at risk from changing hydrological regimes under climate change. Understanding likely future changes in wetland hydrology will help mitigate impacts and guide adaptation strategies for high‐value sites. We used satellite‐based observations of wetland inundation to calibrate conceptual runoff models modified to represent wetland storage dynamics across 34,890 wetlands in the state of Victoria, Australia. Wetlands across Victoria feature a range of hydrologic regimes, from permanent waterbodies to highly episodic systems that inundate only every few years. We assessed future climate‐driven changes in seven wetland ecohydrological metrics used to inform wetland water regime classification for a subset of 11,660 high performing wetland models. By 2075 in a high emissions scenario (SSP3‐7.0), up to 90% of wetlands are projected to change their hydrological regime classification, and the statewide average annual maximum inundated area might reduce by 60%, relative to 1988–2022. The biggest risk is to permanent wetlands, where even under a moderate emissions scenario (SSP2‐4.5) and median climate change projections, over two thirds could transition to seasonal or intermittent systems by 2075. Wetlands with extremely rare inundation and thus low biodiversity and ecosystem benefits are projected to increase nine‐fold under SSP3‐7.0. These projected hydrological regime shifts imply risks to wetland‐dependent species and ecosystem services. Our findings provide a large‐scale and transferable quantitative assessment of climate change impacts on wetland hydrology, highlighting critical vulnerabilities from a drying climate.

articles.title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
articles.titleEn: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
articles.abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

articles.title: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
articles.titleEn: Projected Climate Change Impacts on Deep‐Sea Corals of the Red Sea
articles.abstract: Ocean warming, acidification, and deoxygenation, among other co‐occurring factors, are shifting species ranges throughout the marine environment. Mesophotic and deep corals are understudied in their response to climate changes, particularly in the Red Sea, which has relatively high temperatures and salinities and is projected to undergo major changes in the future, with little assessment of the impacts to date. Ecological niche modelling can be used to explain the known distribution of a species, predict its current range, and estimate future range shift under changing ocean scenarios. Here, we estimate the area of suitable habitat for four mesophotic and deep‐sea corals ( Acanthogorgia spp., Stylaster tritoni, Bathypathes thermophila , and Madracis interjecta ) across the whole Red Sea under present conditions and under different scenarios of future environmental changes (years 2090–2100). We found variations in the responses of these corals, but two of the four taxa are projected to lose significant amounts of their current habitats, while the other two lose a smaller portion. In particular, the scleractinian coral M. interjecta is likely to lose the largest proportion of its habitat, while the black coral B. thermophila may experience the least change. Deeper areas may become suitable for these corals, but colonisation will depend on their ability to disperse. We also assessed the potential biodiversity hotspots both now and in the future, finding the northern Red Sea to be one ecologically important area. These results enable marine spatial planning in support of an effective long‐term conservation action to protect these important habitats.

articles.title: Deadwood Mitigates Declines in Soil Food‐Web Energy Fluxes in Canopy Gaps
articles.titleEn: Deadwood Mitigates Declines in Soil Food‐Web Energy Fluxes in Canopy Gaps
articles.abstract: Across forests worldwide, frequent climate extremes and intensified timber harvest are reshaping forest structure by increasing tree mortality and canopy opening, threatening terrestrial biodiversity and ecosystem sustainability. In unmanaged forests, natural disturbances create canopy gaps and leave substantial deadwood on site, whereas timber harvesting creates gaps through the removal of living trees, thereby limiting the accumulation of deadwood. However, how these disturbances and management practices affect ecosystem functioning, especially of the belowground system, remains little understood. Here, we reconstructed 116 soil animal food webs in a full‐factorial experiment manipulating forest gaps and deadwood addition. We quantified energy fluxes of soil food webs as an integrative measure of belowground ecosystem functioning and investigated their network architecture 2 years after establishment of the experiment. Forest gaps reduced total food web energy fluxes by 13.4%, decreased network connectance, and shifted energy flow towards the bacteria‐dominated “fast” channel, indicating simplified soil food webs, impaired soil functioning, and reduced energy retention belowground. However, compared to gaps without deadwood, the presence of deadwood in gaps increased total energy flux by 37.4%, primarily through enhanced fungivory and wood‐feeding pathways, and restored network connectance and cycling rates to levels comparable to those in closed‐canopy forests. Our results demonstrate that deadwood acts as a key structural component that mitigates the detrimental effects of canopy gap formation on belowground ecosystem functioning, underscoring deadwood retention after timber harvest as a practical strategy to safeguard soil functioning in a more disturbance‐prone future.

articles.title: China's Irrigation‐Induced Evapotranspiration Largely Returns to Land as Precipitation Through Atmospheric Recycling
articles.titleEn: China's Irrigation‐Induced Evapotranspiration Largely Returns to Land as Precipitation Through Atmospheric Recycling
articles.abstract: Irrigation‐induced evapotranspiration (IrrET), the atmospheric flux of irrigation water consumption (IWC), is commonly treated as local freshwater depletion, yet where this water returns as precipitation through atmospheric recycling remains poorly quantified. Here, we develop a high‐resolution estimate of China's IrrET and combine it with Lagrangian moisture tracking to quantify its contribution to local and remote precipitation. This approach identifies where water vapor originating from IrrET contributes to precipitation, rather than simulating the dynamical precipitation response to irrigation. IrrET was estimated from the residual between satellite‐based evapotranspiration and ERA5‐Land baseline evapotranspiration, while accounting for inter‐dataset biases and irrigated cropland fraction. The resulting IrrET estimates showed strong agreement with prefecture‐level IWC statistics after calibration ( R = 0.91, Rbias = −6%, root mean square error = 0.28 km 3 yr −1 ). During 2008–2017, China's IrrET contributed 189.5 km 3 yr −1 to precipitation, of which 65% fell over land, including 47% within China and 18% over neighboring terrestrial regions. Moisture tracking further revealed contrasting regional source–sink relationships, with the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau and Loess Plateau receiving net atmospheric water inputs, whereas the remaining zones acted as net atmospheric water exporters. China's IrrET increased at a rate of 2.8 km 3 yr −2 during 2000–2020, mainly due to irrigated‐area expansion. This increase was associated with an additional 73.6 km 3 of attributed precipitation under fixed climatological source–sink relationships. These results link local irrigation water depletion with regional moisture recycling and show that atmospheric redistribution should be considered when assessing irrigation sustainability in coupled human–water–climate systems.

articles.title: Oil Spill Vulnerability in the Arabian/Persian Gulf Threatens Regional Water Security and Global Energy Supply
articles.titleEn: Oil Spill Vulnerability in the Arabian/Persian Gulf Threatens Regional Water Security and Global Energy Supply
articles.abstract: The Arabian/Persian Gulf contains more than half of the world's proven oil reserves and is a critical hub for global energy transport, yet it faces increasing oil spill risk from intense tanker traffic, geopolitical tensions, and clandestine oil smuggling operations. At the same time, the region is among the most water‐scarce globally and relies heavily on seawater desalination, making desalination plants and oil and gas (O&G) export terminals highly vulnerable to marine oil pollution. Here we combine backward‐in‐time oil spill dispersal simulations for 2016–2022 with marine traffic data to identify offshore areas from which spills are most likely to impact these infrastructures. Oil spill vulnerability shows strong seasonal variability, with northwesterly Shamal winds driving pollution toward the southeastern Gulf, particularly affecting facilities in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Qatar. Two major high‐risk zones emerge: a southwestern corridor linking Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, and the UAE, and a northeastern hotspot along the UAE coastline. We find that about 19% of the Gulf's surface constitutes a high‐risk area from which spilled oil could reach key water or energy infrastructures in less than 3 days. These short transport times highlight the limited window for spill detection and response and underscore the need for improved monitoring, forecasting, and international coordination.

articles.title: Soil Microbes Mediate Contrasting Effects of Plant Diversity on Biotic Resistance and Invasional Meltdown
articles.titleEn: Soil Microbes Mediate Contrasting Effects of Plant Diversity on Biotic Resistance and Invasional Meltdown
articles.abstract: Biological invasions are intensifying worldwide as a major component of global change, with soil microbes increasingly recognized as key regulators of invasion outcomes. Yet how soil microbes interact with biodiversity to determine whether communities resist or facilitate invasion, particularly through their effects on plant growth and species interactions, remains unclear. Here, we conducted a two‐phase feedback experiment in which soils were conditioned across a diversity gradient of native or invasive plant communities. We characterized soil fungal communities and quantified microbial effects on plant growth and species interactions between phylogenetically paired native and invasive species. Biodiversity generated contrasting invasion outcomes depending on community origin, driven by distinct microbial pathways. In native‐conditioned soils, increasing diversity reduced invader dominance (biotic resistance), primarily mediated by microbial effects on interspecific competition that enhanced native competition strength while reducing that of invaders. In contrast, in invasive‐conditioned soils, increasing diversity facilitated invader dominance (invasional meltdown), primarily driven by enhanced invader growth and suppression of natives. These patterns were associated with shifts in key microbial groups. Putative pathogen richness increased with increasing plant diversity and was negatively associated with native growth, whereas AMF richness declined with increasing plant diversity in native communities but increased with increasing plant diversity in invasive communities, promoting invader growth and competition strength. By integrating biodiversity‐ecosystem functioning, biotic resistance, invasional meltdown, and competitive interactions within a plant–soil feedback framework, our study advances invasion ecology. It identifies soil microbes as central mediators that link biodiversity to ecosystem invasibility through distinct pathways affecting plant growth and species interactions.

articles.title: Natural Coastal Protection and Urban Settlement Patterns: A Multi‐Region Analysis of Wave Sheltering Effects on Coastal Urbanization
articles.titleEn: Natural Coastal Protection and Urban Settlement Patterns: A Multi‐Region Analysis of Wave Sheltering Effects on Coastal Urbanization
articles.abstract: Coastal urbanization is accelerating globally, yet the role of natural coastal protection in shaping settlement patterns remains poorly understood. We examine how wave climate influences coastal population distribution by integrating global wave analysis data from the Copernicus Marine Service (CMEMS, January 2023–May 2025) with high‐resolution population metrics (WorldPop) across five geomorphologically diverse coastal regions (Tokyo Bay, Melbourne, New York, Pearl River Delta, Yangtze River Delta). A dual‐model spatial framework—combining a coastal distance‐decay model and a regional neighborhood‐average model—quantifies inland wave influence. Beyond the conventional mean significant wave height, we derive the deep‐water wave energy flux and decompose the wave field into its swell and wind‐sea partitions. In Japan, the swell‐only metrics match or exceed the explanatory power of total‐wave metrics while the wind‐sea component is generally weaker, consistent with a contribution from swell filtering; the relative performance of wave metrics varies among regions. To assess whether this signal could reflect the geometry of flat alluvial terrain, we further compute terrain slope from 30 m SRTM data and report partial correlations controlling for slope; the wave–population relationship persists with only marginal attenuation, indicating that wave climate carries explanatory power beyond terrain geometry alone. The proposed framework offers a physically grounded, quantitative tool for assessing natural coastal resilience and has implications for sustainable urban planning under climate change.

articles.title: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.titleEn: The carbon at risk measure for managing carbon removal risk and guiding portfolio construction
articles.abstract: Carbon removal markets lack a standardized, quantitative measure of permanence risk. Inspired by value at risk in financial markets, we propose carbon at risk (CaR): a probabilistic measure of the shortfall between contracted removals and realized storage at a given confidence level and time horizon. We calibrate CaR in two proof-of-concept applications: forest carbon, where Monte Carlo simulations driven by satellite fire data yield a single-project 95% CaR of more than 70% over 200 years for California, and geological storage, where simulations using the Storage Security Calculator show that the 95% CaR ranges from 0.15% (well-regulated offshore) to 17% (poorly regulated onshore). Combining technologies in a portfolio can help manage tail risk cost-effectively. The minimum cost of meeting a permanence target depends on the magnitude and correlation structure of key risk factors. CaR provides a technology-agnostic basis for risk-calibrated buffer sizing, insurance pricing and reserve-fund design, over both policy- and climate-relevant horizons.

articles.title: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive
articles.titleEn: A biofilm-derived peptide as an underwater adhesive
articles.abstract: Wet adhesives that perform under water have broad applications in industrial and biomedical settings. To date, molecular designs for underwater adhesives have largely been inspired by marine animals including mussels and barnacles. Here, we propose bacterial biofilms as an alternative source of inspiration for underwater adhesives. Specifically, we demonstrate the application potential of a peptide derived from biofilms formed by the notorious pathogen Vibrio cholerae . We characterize the ability of this biofilm-derived peptide to adsorb onto various surfaces and to glue wet surfaces by using a combination of confocal microscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, atomic force microscopy, lap shear tests, and spectroscopic tools. We further show that the peptide can coaggregate with microspheres acting as an effective flocculant. Our results open new design possibilities for underwater adhesives inspired by natural biofilms.

articles.title: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO2 tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
articles.titleEn: Elevated early Eocene atmospheric CO2 tied to reduced Southern Ocean biological pump efficiency
articles.abstract: The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum (53 to 49 million years ago) was an interval in Earth’s history when reconstructed temperatures and atmospheric CO 2 concentrations were among the highest of the Cenozoic Era (that is, the last 66 million years). The causes of the high CO 2 levels remain unclear. CO 2 changes over recent ice age cycles appear to be largely controlled by the biologically mediated build-up and release of carbon from the Southern Ocean, a process that might have also played a role earlier in the Cenozoic. Here we test this possibility with foraminifera-bound nitrogen isotope measurements. Our data show higher surface nitrate concentrations in the Southern Ocean, and thus a more inefficient biological sequestration of carbon during peak Early Eocene Climatic Optimum. The associated transfer of CO 2 from the deep ocean to the atmosphere would have been amplified by the low seawater buffering capacity of the Eocene, due to the lower pH and high Ca ion concentration. Previously proposed low silicate rock weatherability during the Eocene may have weakened the weathering thermostat, allowing the reconstructed change in biological pump efficiency in the Southern Ocean to explain at least half of the atmospheric CO 2 increase observed during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum.

articles.title: Earth system modelling of mercury using CESM2 – Part 3: Oceanic model POP2/Hg v1.0
articles.titleEn: Earth system modelling of mercury using CESM2 – Part 3: Oceanic model POP2/Hg v1.0
articles.abstract: Mercury (Hg) is a globally distributed toxicant with complex cycling in the ocean, involving redox reactions, air–sea exchange, and microbial methylation. We present POP2/Hg v1.0, a new global ocean mercury model developed within the ocean component of CESM2 (POP2) and coupled to the Marine Biogeochemistry Library (MARBL). POP2/Hg v1.0 simulates dissolved elemental Hg (Hg 0 ), oxidized Hg (Hg II ), particulate-bound Hg (Hg P ), and methylmercury (MeHg = MMHg + DMHg), linking their transformation to ecosystem processes and dynamics of particulate organic carbon (POC). The model captures observed large-scale features of marine Hg. Surface Hg 0 concentrations range from 0.01 to 0.12 pmol L −1 (pM, 1 pM = 10 −12 mol L −1 ) and are elevated in tropical and subtropical oceans due to strong photoreduction and limited evasion. Subsurface Hg 0 maxima emerge in upwelling zones, reflecting remineralization-driven Hg II reduction. Surface Hg II concentrations peak in regions of high atmospheric deposition and productivity and rise at depth in oxygen-deficient zones. Hg P is closely associated with high POC and Hg II levels in the surface ocean but attenuates rapidly with depth due to remineralization. MeHg accumulates in the subsurface and deep sea, broadly consistent with observations. Total Hg (Hg T ) at surface generally falls within the range of open-ocean observations, with values of 0.1–1.0 pM across most regions and localized concentrations exceeding 1.2 pM. The biological pump strongly shapes vertical Hg transport. Above 1000 m, soft POC carries 98.55 % of Hg P flux, driving export and remineralization. Below 1000 m, hard POC becomes relatively more important and accounts for 43.94 % of the integrated Hg P flux reaching seafloor cells, locally contributing up to over 99 %, although the total flux is small (16.86 Mg yr −1 ). Sensitivity tests show that altering redox rates significantly affects the vertical distribution of Hg transformations. Reduced surface reduction and oxidation rates increase Hg 0 concentrations in the upper ocean, decrease Hg II concentrations, and weaken seasonal variability. By embedding mercury chemistry into a biogeochemical and physical ocean model which can be potentially fully coupled, POP2/Hg v1.0 offers a process-resolving platform for assessing mercury cycling and its response to environmental change. It enables future integrated Earth system simulations and provides a foundation for simulating marine mercury under future climate and policy scenarios.

articles.title: Daily global sea surface ageostrophic current dataset from 1993–2023 via physics-informed deep learning
articles.titleEn: Daily global sea surface ageostrophic current dataset from 1993–2023 via physics-informed deep learning
articles.abstract: Surface ocean circulation shapes climate, air–sea exchange, and the transport of heat, carbon, and other tracers, yet most long-term global datasets rely primarily on geostrophic balance and therefore miss important ageostrophic motions. Here, we reconstruct global daily sea surface circulation at 0.25° resolution from 1993 to 2023 using a physics-informed framework that integrates satellite altimetry with momentum constraints from geostrophic balance, wind stress, and nonlinear advection (Cui, 2026; https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19966716). The resulting dataset is dynamically consistent, with a mean momentum balance error below 1.5 %, and reduces the median velocity error against independent mooring observations across the tropical Pacific, Atlantic, and Indian Oceans to 0.07 m s −1 , compared with 0.20 m s −1 for geostrophic currents and 0.10 m s −1 for Ekman corrected currents. We show that geostrophic flow sets the large-scale circulation, whereas Ekman and nonlinear contributions are smaller but comparable in magnitude to each other. Although nonlinear advection contributes little to relative vorticity, it strongly shapes surface divergence and the fine scale structure of eddy kinetic energy. Our results show that nonlinear ageostrophic flow is an essential component of global surface circulation and that neglecting it limits our ability to resolve surface transport and variability on climatically relevant scales.

articles.title: Climate Warming Reduces Seed Mass in European Beech Through Altered Resource Dynamics and Drought
articles.titleEn: Climate Warming Reduces Seed Mass in European Beech Through Altered Resource Dynamics and Drought
articles.abstract: Seed mass is a key life‐history trait that influences dispersal, seedling establishment, and plant fitness, yet its long‐term response to climate change remains poorly understood. We used two long‐term datasets of European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) from the United Kingdom (1989–2024) and the Netherlands (1976–2024) to test whether seed mass has changed over time and whether any decline can be attributed to changing climate or altered resource dynamics. Seed mass declined by 13% over the study period, with a non‐linear decrease starting in the mid‐2000s. Models of year‐to‐year variation showed that seeds were smaller in years with lower reconstructed stored resources and in years that early summer was dry. Temporal contribution analysis indicated that the long‐term decline in seed mass was driven primarily by declining resource availability, with increasing drought making an additional contribution. Climate warming affects seed size in beech by direct effects of drought on seed development, and indirectly by altering reproductive dynamics and shortening the intervals available for resource recovery between reproductive events. Because seed mass influences dispersal and survival of seeds and seedlings, declines in seed mass are likely to reduce regeneration potential. Our findings identify an indirect pathway by which climate change may weaken forest regeneration.

articles.title: Microbial Life‐History Strategies Shape Biocrusts Soil Multifunctionality Responses to Multi‐Year Snow‐Cover Change
articles.titleEn: Microbial Life‐History Strategies Shape Biocrusts Soil Multifunctionality Responses to Multi‐Year Snow‐Cover Change
articles.abstract: Winter snowfall is a critical water source sustaining the survival and ecological functioning of biocrusts in desert ecosystems, yet how different biocrust types respond to altered snow‐depth conditions and maintain soil multifunctionality (SMF) through microbial community adjustments and life‐history strategies remains poorly understood. Based on a field snow‐manipulation experiment, we compared SMF responses in cyanobacterial and lichen crusts under snow removal, ambient snow, and double‐snow treatments across different treatment‐duration categories and further explored the underlying microbial regulatory mechanisms. Cyanobacterial and lichen crusts exhibited contrasting SMF responses to altered snow conditions. SMF significantly increased in cyanobacterial crusts in the short‐term treatment plots (1 year), whereas lichen crusts showed a significant decline only under short‐term snow removal. In the medium‐ and long‐term treatment plots (8 and 11 years), differences in SMF between altered‐snow and ambient‐snow conditions were reduced for both biocrust types. Lichen crusts mainly showed increases in bacterial and total microbial diversity under snow manipulation, whereas significant diversity responses in cyanobacterial crusts were primarily associated with fungi. Microbial life‐history strategies showed clear but biocrust‐type‐specific associations with SMF. Random forest and structural equation modeling (SEM) analyses indicated that SMF in cyanobacterial crusts was strongly constrained by the S strategy, while Y‐related metabolic pathways were positively associated with SMF; in contrast, SMF in lichen crusts was positively associated with the A strategy but negatively associated with the S strategy. Soil physicochemical properties also played an important role in regulating SMF, but their effects and interactions with microbial attributes differed between the two biocrust types. Overall, this study demonstrates that altered snow conditions regulate biocrust SMF through the coupling of soil environmental changes and microbial functional responses, with the underlying regulatory pathways strongly dependent on biocrust type.

articles.title: Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya
articles.titleEn: Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya
articles.abstract: Environmental impacts endured by the Lowland Maya during the Classic Period (250 to 920 CE) included droughts, deforestation, and soil erosion. Recent studies on mercury (Hg) pollution and cyanotoxins suggest that degraded water quality was also a stressor for the Pre-Columbian Maya. Hg in the Maya region is related to use of both elemental mercury and mineral cinnabar (HgS), the latter used as a red pigment. Questions, however, remain concerning the toxicity of Hg or the consequences of prehistoric Hg exposure on ecosystem and human health. Here, we show that Classic Period Hg concentrations in sediment cores from two lakes on the Yucatán Peninsula exceeded modern sediment Hg toxicity thresholds by orders of magnitude for centuries during ancient Maya occupation. Sediments also have evidence of aquatic food web collapse (algae, bacteria, cyanobacteria, ostracods, snails, and nonbiting midges), coincident with the time of high Hg concentrations, confirming that Hg toxicity was an additional environmental stressor for Classic Maya populations.

articles.title: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
articles.titleEn: A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression
articles.abstract: Identifying the neurobiological basis of cognitive vulnerability is essential for preventing Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We derived the Alzheimer’s Resilience-Vulnerability Connectome (ARC) by contrasting SuperAgers (SA), an extreme phenotype of preserved late-life memory, with AD using resting-state fMRI. ARC distinguished SA from AD in a discovery cohort ( N = 290; AUC = 0.85) and replicated independently ( N = 143), involving prefrontal, temporal, and insular networks and associating with brain age. Applied to cognitively unimpaired adults (discovery: N = 818; replication: N = 497), ARC-based subtyping revealed SA-like and AD-like subgroups with comparable baseline cognition but divergent longitudinal trajectories. AD-like individuals exhibited faster cognitive decline, greater amyloid-β accumulation, and higher AD conversion risk. Exploratory GWAS nominated CLYBL and FRMD6 as candidate novel loci associated with the subtype difference. These findings suggest that ARC captures a continuous connectomic dimension of cognitive aging spanning SA, cognitively typical aging, and AD, highlighting the potential of functional connectomic variation for early risk stratification in AD.

articles.title: METTL3-mediated m 6 A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression
articles.titleEn: METTL3-mediated m 6 A modification of DNMT1 enhances ovarian cancer progression
articles.abstract: High-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), the most lethal subtype of ovarian cancer, is often diagnosed at advanced stages and remains associated with poor clinical outcome. In this study, we identify a critical oncogenic role of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) RNA modification pathway in HGSOC. Suppression of METTL3, either genetically or pharmacologically, and depletion of its binding partner METTL14 impair ovarian cancer proliferation and tumor progression. Mechanistically, we show that METTL3-mediated m 6 A deposition enhances the translation of DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1), the primary maintenance DNA methyltransferase responsible for preserving genome-wide methylation patterns and silencing tumor suppressor genes. Pharmacological inhibition of DNMT1 induces widespread DNA hypomethylation and up-regulation of the tumor suppressors TNFAIP3 and FBXO32. Consistently, METTL3 suppression reduces DNMT1 abundance and derepresses TNFAIP3 and FBXO32 expression. Knockdown and rescue studies further reveal that DNMT1 primarily mediates METTL3-dependent regulation of cell migration, whereas the antiproliferative effects of METTL3 suppression are likely driven by additional downstream targets. Collectively, these findings identify the m 6 A-METTL3-DNMT1 axis as a mechanistic link between RNA and DNA methylation pathways and a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HGSOC.

articles.title: Three-way circulation–soil moisture–temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
articles.titleEn: Three-way circulation–soil moisture–temperature feedbacks amplify the most extreme mid-latitudinal heat waves
articles.abstract: The most extreme heat waves are intensifying faster than moderate events across many mid-latitude regions. Climate models underestimate these trends, suggesting an incomplete representation and understanding of the underlying physical processes. Here, we use an explainable machine-learning framework to investigate interactions among atmospheric circulation, surface soil moisture, and temperature, and their role in recent heat extremes. We show that a three-way interaction among these components becomes active once a critical temperature threshold is exceeded, contributing, on average, ∼10% to peak temperature anomalies during the most extreme heat events across ∼28% of humid mid-latitude regions. We further reveal that this interaction is systematically underestimated in CMIP6 and CESM2 Large Ensemble simulations. Soils in climate models are too dry at the initiation of heat waves, therefore suppressing subsequent soil-moisture depletion and inhibiting feedback activation. These findings help explain regional model biases in upper-tail warming and highlight avenues for improving future projections of extreme heat events.

articles.title: Human carotid plaque risk imaging using multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound fusion (hCAPRI)
articles.titleEn: Human carotid plaque risk imaging using multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound fusion (hCAPRI)
articles.abstract: Assessing the risk of carotid plaque rupture remains limited because current imaging methods cannot provide both plaque composition and structural information in real time. Here, we present human carotid plaque risk imaging (hCAPRI), a multiparametric photoacoustic and ultrasound (PA/US) fusion method for real-time carotid plaque assessment. hCAPRI combines PA imaging for detecting intraplaque hemorrhage (IPH) with US imaging for evaluating the plaque structure. PA imaging measured IPH size and methemoglobin content, while US imaging assessed stenosis severity, calcification, and plaque thickness. Combining these PA/US parameters, we compute an hCAPRI score. In 171 carotid arteries (CAs) from 120 patients, hCAPRI revealed the relationships among the PA/US parameters. In 36 CAs validated with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), hCAPRI showed high agreement with MRI. The hCAPRI score achieved 89% sensitivity and 84% specificity for high-risk plaque classification. hCAPRI offers a low-cost, real-time, and contrast-free approach for carotid plaque risk imaging.

articles.title: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
articles.titleEn: Measuring mixed-state topological invariant in open photonic quantum walk
articles.abstract: Pure-state manifestations of geometric phase are well established and have found applications across essentially all branches of physics, yet their generalization to mixed-state regimes remains largely unexplored experimentally. The Uhlmann geometric phase offers a natural extension of pure-state paradigms and can exhibit a topological character. However, observation of this invariant is impeded by the incompatibility between Uhlmann parallel transport and Hamiltonian dynamics, as well as the difficulty of preparing topologically nontrivial mixed states. To address this challenge, we report an experimentally accessible protocol for directly measuring the mixed-state topological invariant. By engineering controlled nonunitary dynamics in a photonic quantum walk, we prepare topologically nontrivial mixed states from a trivial initial state. Then, by machine learning the full density matrix in momentum space, we directly extract the quantized geometric phase of the nontrivial mixed states. Furthermore, we observe that this transition of the quantized mixed-state topological invariant from a trivial to a nontrivial value is closely associated with the emergence of a topological kink structure. These results highlight a geometric phase framework that naturally extends to open quantum systems both in and out of thermal equilibrium.

articles.title: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
articles.titleEn: Stony coral symbioses show variable responses to future ocean conditions
articles.abstract: Coral reefs support over a quarter of marine species and nearly a billion people worldwide but are also among the ecosystems most threatened by anthropogenic impacts. There is long-standing debate about whether coral symbioses will be disrupted or respond adaptively under future ocean conditions. Using a factorial 2.5-year future-ocean mesocosm experiment across eight coral species representing the major coral lineages, we tracked symbiont community shifts within replicate fragments from the same individual coral. Some corals exhibited stochastic divergence, whereas others showed deterministic shifts in symbiont community composition. Heat stress generally reduced symbiont diversity and promoted predictable restructuring, consistent with deterministic adaptation to moderate thermal stress but stochastic accumulation of diversity under extreme conditions. We propose that adaptive and stochastic responses represent endpoints along a continuum of host-orchestrated symbiont sorting. This study bridges coral reef ecology with broader host-microbiome theory, offering an integrated perspective on how symbiotic systems may respond to environmental change.

articles.title: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
articles.titleEn: Clinically derived micro- and nanoplastic uptake drives spatiotemporally confined metabolic stress revealed by bond-selective imaging
articles.abstract: Although microplastics and nanoplastics (MPs/NPs) are pervasive environmental contaminants, our understanding of cellular toxicity remains incomplete, as adverse effects are often attributed to long-term intracellular accumulation, while the spatiotemporal onset of cellular damage remains poorly defined. Here, we use chemical bond–selective stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy and cell models that decouple continuous exposure from intracellular retention to directly visualize clinically derived MP/NP-cell interactions. Cellular stress occurs primarily during MP/NP exposure, accompanied by alterations in lipid droplet (LD) composition. In contrast, following extracellular removal, intracellularly retained MP/NP become largely inert, with recovery of lipid metabolism and cellular functions. Lipidomics identifies arachidonic acid (AA) as a key dysregulated metabolite, and SRS imaging further reveals transient, spatially confined AA enrichment in MP/NP–proximal LDs during uptake. Phospholipid coating of MP/NP attenuates LD alterations and cytotoxicity while preserving particle internalization, establishing uptake-driven metabolic stress, rather than long-term intracellular retention, as a primary source of MP/NP–induced damage.

articles.title: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
articles.titleEn: Identification of a specialized lipid barrier for Drosophila metamorphosis
articles.abstract: Many terrestrial insects transition from humid to dry environments at metamorphosis, yet how they avoid dehydration is unclear. In Drosophila melanogaster , we identify a lipid barrier to water loss in the pupa that is anatomically distinct from that of the adult. It comprises unisex hydrocarbons that are longer and less volatile than their sex-specific adult counterparts. These hyperlong hydrocarbons are produced by larval oenocytes and stored in the fat body for subsequent transport to the cuticle at pupariation. A fatty acid elongase, EloHL, is required for hyperlong hydrocarbon biosynthesis and for a functional barrier to dehydration during early metamorphosis. Hyperlong barrier hydrocarbons are widespread across the Drosophila genus and typically transition to shorter sex-specific versions during adult maturation. In the desert species D. mojavensis , however, adults retain hyperlong hydrocarbons. This study reveals how insect lipid barriers are tuned to environmental variations in aridity and temperature during development and evolution.

articles.title: Exploring Air–Sea Interactions in a Regional Weakly Coupled Data Assimilation System: An Observing System Experiment for the 2023 Indian Ocean Monsoon and Cyclone Biparjoy
articles.titleEn: Exploring Air–Sea Interactions in a Regional Weakly Coupled Data Assimilation System: An Observing System Experiment for the 2023 Indian Ocean Monsoon and Cyclone Biparjoy
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: We examined air–sea interactions in a weakly coupled ocean–atmosphere data assimilation (DA) system by performing an observing system experiment (OSE). The OSE is performed for the Arabian Sea monsoon onset event in 2023, which also coincides with the passage of the tropical cyclone Biparjoy. Results show that assimilating both oceanic and atmospheric data produces a better forecast of the ocean–atmosphere state (fit to the assimilated data) than either experiment assimilating only oceanic or atmospheric data. This indicates that the coupled system provides more consistent initial conditions, yielding more balanced oceanic and atmospheric states when assimilating all the data. However, we found that assimilating only atmospheric data improves both the ocean and atmosphere state forecasts, whereas assimilating only oceanic data improves the ocean state forecasts but degrades the atmospheric state forecasts, when compared with the free run (coupled model simulation without assimilating any data). We found that this counterintuitive model performance is due to the systematic misrepresentation of air–sea exchanges. First, errors in the cyclone path increase when atmospheric data are not assimilated. Then, assimilation of sea surface temperature (SST) leads to a warmer SST below the misplaced cyclone (with cyclone path offset of about 200 km relative to IBTrACS data), resulting in increased cyclone intensity. This misrepresentation of air–sea exchanges not only occurs during the cyclone passage but also persists throughout the early monsoon season. Since errors in one component can affect the other and result in positive feedback, leading to error growth, this study highlights an interesting effect on weakly coupled ocean–atmosphere DA systems when atmospheric data are unavailable or limited in space and time, particularly during high‐impact atmospheric events such as tropical cyclones.

articles.title: Improvement of a Regional Multiscale NLS‐4DVar Assimilation System Based on the CWRF‐CoLM Coupled Model
articles.titleEn: Improvement of a Regional Multiscale NLS‐4DVar Assimilation System Based on the CWRF‐CoLM Coupled Model
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Ensemble perturbations in 4DEnVar‐type methods are pulled in two directions at once: estimating a reliable background‐error covariance (BEC) calls for perturbations large enough to sample real error structure, while a valid tangent‐linear (TL) approximation calls for perturbations small enough to stay near‐linear. This study resolves this conflict by introducing a shrinkage factor () into a multigrid NLS‐4DVar framework, decoupling the perturbation scale used for BEC estimation from that used for TL approximation. An independent finite‐difference test verifies this decoupling, showing that TL accuracy is governed by a trade‐off between nonlinear truncation error and numerical error. Based on this framework, an improved Regional Multiscale Nonlinear Least Squares (NLS) 4DVar Data Assimilation System was developed based on the CWRF‐CoLM coupled model. A 1‐month cycling assimilation experiment (July 2021) shows that the new scheme (DA2) outperforms the original (DA1): analysis RMSE and bias are reduced for U / V winds, T , and QVAPOR, 3‐day forecast RMSE improves broadly, and the 24‐hr precipitation threat score at moderate‐to‐heavy rainfall thresholds is notably higher, which is consistent with a preferential benefit for strongly nonlinear moisture and convective processes. Although only atmospheric observations are assimilated, land‐surface forecasts (2‐m temperature, 2‐m humidity, soil moisture) also improve indirectly, driven by a more accurate initial moisture field and better‐represented land‐atmosphere coupling. Beyond its practical performance, this decoupling strategy completes a previously unverified aspect of the NLS‐4DVar formulation and offers a generalizable approach for mitigating nonlinear errors in ensemble‐based variational assimilation.

articles.title: Machine Learning‐Based Representation of Model Error and Observation Error With Estimated Cross‐Correlation in Data Assimilation
articles.titleEn: Machine Learning‐Based Representation of Model Error and Observation Error With Estimated Cross‐Correlation in Data Assimilation
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: The current study presents machine learning (ML)‐based schemes that independently represent model error and observation error during data assimilation. The Model Error ML scheme (MLME) uses a generative adversarial network (GAN) to produce flow‐dependent model corrections. The Observation Error ML scheme (MLOE) also uses the GAN to adaptively estimate the observation error covariance matrix. Furthermore, a generalized formulation (CorrFOE) is derived to incorporate the often‐neglected cross‐correlations between forecast and observation errors. The proposed schemes are rigorously evaluated via twin experiments with the Lorenz III model. Results show that the ML‐based schemes reduce the root‐mean‐square error (RMSE) of analyses relative to the control and, for model error, relative to the additive‐noise baseline. Additionally, the MLME scheme is particularly effective at recovering small‐scale structures. Crucially, the synergistic combination of both ML schemes with the explicit inclusion of cross‐correlation between forecast and observation errors produces the most accurate analyses. The added computational costs for MLME, MLOE and CorrFOE are moderate, confirming their operational potential.

articles.title: Physics‐Informed Neural Networks as Differentiable Surrogates for 4D‐Variational Data Assimilation
articles.titleEn: Physics‐Informed Neural Networks as Differentiable Surrogates for 4D‐Variational Data Assimilation
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Biogeochemical forecasting requires state estimation methods that accommodate sparse observations, nonlinear dynamics, and discontinuous ecological processes. Four‐dimensional variational data assimilation addresses this challenge but depends on tangent‐linear and adjoint models that are costly to derive and maintain alongside evolving forward codes, and that are not defined where biogeochemical formulations are non‐differentiable. We propose a framework in which a physics‐informed neural network (PINN) replaces the traditional numerical model and its linearizations, remaining differentiable through automatic differentiation while embedding simplified governing equations as structural guardrails and computing the forward, tangent‐linear, and adjoint operators simultaneously from a single computational graph. Applied to nitrate‐phytoplankton‐zooplankton dynamics as a controlled testbed, our approach achieves an approximately six‐fold speedup over traditional numerical models in twin experiments while maintaining comparable state estimation accuracy across observation sampling scenarios. Jacobian analysis shows that the learned sensitivities are consistent with the embedded ecological relationships where these agree with the data, while departing where simplified formulations prove inadequate. This framework demonstrates that PINN‐based surrogates can maintain dynamical consistency in variational data assimilation while reducing implementation burden, offering a path toward more flexible and maintainable forecasting systems for increasingly complex biogeochemical models.

articles.title: An Unstructured Voronoi Mesh Framework for Large‐Scale Hydrologic and Land Surface Models
articles.titleEn: An Unstructured Voronoi Mesh Framework for Large‐Scale Hydrologic and Land Surface Models
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Accurate representation of river networks and land surface heterogeneity is crucial for improving the performance of continental‐to‐global hydrologic and land surface models. Traditional approaches rely on either coarse‐resolution grids, which may oversimplify complex terrain and limit the accurate representation of key processes, or computationally demanding full‐domain high‐resolution meshes. This study expands upon our previous research on unstructured mesh‐based hydrologic modeling by introducing a novel framework for generating Hydrologic Refined Meshes (HRMs). This framework seamlessly integrates crucial land surface features, including river networks, watershed boundaries, and lake boundaries, into the mesh generation process. The HRM framework provides a generalized, feature‐driven workflow for strategic mesh refinement; here, we implement it within the Model for Prediction Across Scales architecture, leveraging its Centroidal Voronoi Tessellations properties and dual‐grid topology. The resulting variable‐resolution (4–50 km) Voronoi mesh accurately captures these features, demonstrating significant advantages in representing land surface heterogeneity. For instance, the mesh effectively captures surface elevation, resolving most key landscape features despite using nearly half the cell count. River networks are accurately represented by high‐resolution cells aligned along their courses, resulting in a conceptual network that deviates by only approximately on average from the true river network. We demonstrate the applicability of this framework and evaluate the generated mesh using several key variables, including surface elevation and river networks.

articles.title: New Representation of Sea Ice Salt Dynamics in NEMO‐SI 3 v5: Evaluation and Impacts
articles.titleEn: New Representation of Sea Ice Salt Dynamics in NEMO‐SI 3 v5: Evaluation and Impacts
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Although many large‐scale sea ice models now represent salt dynamics, few studies have evaluated them, and uncertainty remains regarding key parameterization choices. Here, we conduct global 1° ocean–ice simulations with NEMO‐SI 3 v5, forced by climatological atmospheric data, tuned to the salinity–thickness relationship, and evaluated against more than 1,400 ice cores. Simulations investigate (a) the treatment of vertical ice salinity variations (diagnostic vs. prognostic), (b) gravity drainage physics (brine fraction‐based vs. Rayleigh number‐based), and (c) key parameter values. On average, ice salinity is simulated within 0.1 g/kg (Arctic) and 0.7 g/kg (Antarctic) of observations, capturing large‐scale features including the Arctic–Antarctic contrast, seasonality, vertical profile, and the salinity–thickness relationship. Using a high value for the new ice liquid fraction parameter is critical for simulating high salinity in the thin ice range. Vertically‐resolved salt dynamics generally outperform the diagnostic approach, consistently across hemispheres, seasons, depth and thickness. Brine fraction‐based and Rayleigh number‐based parameterizations of gravity drainage produce different salinity fields, both through direct effects and interactions with melt ponds. However, limited observational constraints on measurement biases prevent firm conclusions on which approach performs best. Uncertainties in ice salinity are generally larger in the Antarctic than in the Arctic. While salt dynamics strongly affect sea ice mass and salt budget terms, they affect sea ice volume moderately, and have little effect on ocean salinity due to compensating effects.

articles.title: Impacts of Convective Microphysics Parameterization on MJO Simulation in E3SM
articles.titleEn: Impacts of Convective Microphysics Parameterization on MJO Simulation in E3SM
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: This study investigates the impact of convective microphysics parameterization on the simulation of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). Specifically, the two‐moment, five‐class convective microphysics parameterization (CMP) scheme from Song et al. (2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2024ms004656 ) was implemented into Zhang and McFarlane (1995, https://doi.org/10.1080/07055900.1995.9649539 ) convection scheme in E3SM. Results from 15 years of simulations demonstrate that the CMP improves the MJO simulation, particularly in terms of amplitude, period, propagation, life cycle, and seasonality. Wavenumber‐frequency spectra analysis reveals that, with the CMP, the simulated energy peak shifts from 80–180 days to 30–80 days, better aligning with observations. Composite MJO life cycle analysis shows that the CMP enhances precipitation amplitude, eastward propagation, and coherence with zonal winds, addressing weaknesses in the standard model, such as a weak MJO amplitude and delayed propagation. Additionally, in summer, the CMP allows E3SM to better capture the seasonal variation of MJO convective systems, particularly the northward shift in the Asian monsoon region. The CMP enhances MJO convection, making it stronger, and promotes pre‐conditioning east of the MJO convective center, favoring eastward propagation. Model‐process‐oriented diagnostics reveal that the CMP influences the MJO through complex interactions among convection, stratiform clouds, and circulation.
articles.abstractEn: This study investigates the impact of convective microphysics parameterization on the simulation of the Madden–Julian Oscillation (MJO) in the Energy Exascale Earth System Model (E3SM). Specifically, the two‐moment, five‐class convective microphysics parameterization (CMP) scheme from Song et al. (2025, https://doi.org/10.1029/2024ms004656 ) was implemented into Zhang and McFarlane (1995, https://doi.org/10.1080/07055900.1995.9649539 ) convection scheme in E3SM. Results from 15 years of simulations demonstrate that the CMP improves the MJO simulation, particularly in terms of amplitude, period, propagation, life cycle, and seasonality. Wavenumber‐frequency spectra analysis reveals that, with the CMP, the simulated energy peak shifts from 80–180 days to 30–80 days, better aligning with observations. Composite MJO life cycle analysis shows that the CMP enhances precipitation amplitude, eastward propagation, and coherence with zonal winds, addressing weaknesses in the standard model, such as a weak MJO amplitude and delayed propagation. Additionally, in summer, the CMP allows E3SM to better capture the seasonal variation of MJO convective systems, particularly the northward shift in the Asian monsoon region. The CMP enhances MJO convection, making it stronger, and promotes pre‐conditioning east of the MJO convective center, favoring eastward propagation. Model‐process‐oriented diagnostics reveal that the CMP influences the MJO through complex interactions among convection, stratiform clouds, and circulation.

articles.title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
articles.titleEn: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
articles.abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

articles.title: Emissions Poised to Rocket: Modeling the Environmental Impacts of Low Earth Orbit Satellite Constellations
articles.titleEn: Emissions Poised to Rocket: Modeling the Environmental Impacts of Low Earth Orbit Satellite Constellations
articles.abstract: The proliferation of satellite megaconstellations in low Earth orbit represents a significant advancement in global broadband connectivity. However, we urgently need to understand the potential environmental impacts, particularly greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions associated with these constellations. This study addresses a critical gap in modeling current and future GHG emissions by developing an open‐source life cycle assessment methodology, applied to 12 launch vehicles and 24 megaconstellations. Our analysis reveals that fully deploying the 24 constellations would emit about 9.1 Mt CO 2 . Propellant combustion during launch events (60.9%) and launcher production (31.6%) contribute most significantly to overall GHG emissions, accounting for 92.5% of modeled life cycle emissions. Reusing launch vehicles lowers production emissions per launch by 81%–97% relative to building a new vehicle for every flight, highlighting the environmental benefits of reusability in space technology. The findings underscore the importance of launch vehicle and satellite design choices to minimize potential environmental impacts. The Open‐source Rocket and Constellation Lifecycle Emissions (ORACLE) repository is freely available and aims to facilitate further research in this field. This study provides a critical baseline for policymakers and industry stakeholders to develop strategies for reducing the carbon footprint of the space industry, especially satellite megaconstellations.

articles.title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
articles.titleEn: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
articles.abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

articles.title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
articles.titleEn: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
articles.abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

articles.title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
articles.titleEn: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
articles.abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

articles.title: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
articles.titleEn: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
articles.abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

articles.title: Dam-regulated flow fragmentation and sand-mining-driven threshold shifts shorten the Mekong–Tonle Sap reverse-flow season
articles.titleEn: Dam-regulated flow fragmentation and sand-mining-driven threshold shifts shorten the Mekong–Tonle Sap reverse-flow season
articles.abstract: Sand mining, dam construction, and climate change have profoundly altered the hydrological dynamics of the Mekong River-Tonle Sap Lake floodplain system, one of the world's most ecologically productive river-lake complexes. This study provides an integrated, multi-scale assessment of flow regime alteration across the Mekong mainstream and its coupling with the Tonle Sap Lake across three periods: pre-dam (1976–1991), transition (1992–2009), and post-dam (2010–2024). Using daily and sub-daily data from eight mainstream stations, we quantify shifts in long-term flow memory, short-term variability, and flow amplitude. We use a hydrodynamic response-time model to link upstream regime change to the Mekong–Tonle Sap flow exchange. During the post-dam period, flow memory increased in the upper mainstream but decreased slightly downstream, indicating growing upstream–downstream divergence in flow-regime characteristics and increasing hydrological fragmentation. Upstream stations, particularly Chiang Saen, exhibit a 33.3 % increase in minimum flows and a 40 % decrease in maximum flows during the post-dam period compared to the pre-dam period, alongside higher flow memory (+0.11), reflecting flow smoothing by reservoir operations. At the most downstream station at Kratie, a key control point for Tonle Sap inflow, maximum flows decreased by 9.4 %, while minimum flows increased by 117 % relative to the pre-dam baseline; the seasonal timing of peak discharge was also delayed by approximately two to three weeks. Critically, the combined effects of the altered mainstream flow regime and sand-mining-driven riverbed lowering have shifted the conditions under which Tonle Sap flow reversal initiates. Using the lag-adjusted Kratie discharge at onset as a proxy for the Mekong-Tonle Sap confluence stage/head condition, we find that the median onset discharge increased from ∼ 3200 m 3 s −1 (pre-dam) to ∼ 4300 m 3 s −1 under the post-dam fixed-bed scenario (2010–2024 hydrology with reference morphology), and to ∼ 7200 m 3 s −1 once sand-mining-driven channel incision is added. This indicates that post-2010 hydrological alteration reduced the probability of exceeding the discharge threshold for initiating reverse flow, while sand-mining-driven riverbed lowering substantially amplified this shift by modifying local stage–discharge relationships. Together, these interacting drivers shorten the reverse-flow season by approximately 28 d relative to the pre-dam baseline. Sustaining the Mekong–Tonle Sap flood pulse will therefore require basin-wide monitoring and transboundary governance that address flow timing and variability, not volume alone.

articles.title: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.titleEn: Past and future projected radiative effects from irrigation
articles.abstract: Irrigation is the most dominant freshwater use practice on Earth, yet its effect on the top-of-atmosphere (TOA) radiative budget remains uncertain because past estimates have relied on idealised experiments or single-model frameworks. Here, we use historical simulations (1902–2014) from the Irrigation Model Intercomparison Project (IRRMIP) to provide the first multi-model quantification of irrigation-induced effective radiative forcing (ERF), defined as the change in net TOA radiative flux including rapid atmospheric adjustments. Across seven Earth system models, under prescribed sea surface temperatures (SST), the global multi-model mean (MMM) irrigation-induced ERF is positive but small (∼ 0.023 W m −2 ). While the global signal is small, it masks regional heterogeneity: South Asia and West Central Asia exhibit higher positive ERF (∼0.23 W m −2 ), with spatial maps revealing coherent forcing hotspots of up to +5 W m −2 over the Indo-Gangetic Plain that are consistent across all models, while East Asia shows negative ERF (∼-0.03 W m −2 ). The clear-sky ERF is greater than the all-sky ERF in most of the regions, indicating that cloud adjustments following irrigation may exert a negative contribution to the ERF. Correlations between historical irrigation ERF variability and its potential drivers suggest that reduced outgoing longwave radiation is the dominant control at the global scale, as well as in South Asia and West Central Asia, while near-surface temperature, precipitable water, albedo, and cloud cover contribute with substantial regional and inter-model variability. We additionally examine future changes in net TOA radiation imbalance (Δ R n,TOA ) from a fully coupled CMIP-style model (SSP1-2.6 and SSP3-7.0, 2015–2070) to assess whether the historical ERF pattern persists under future irrigation. The global mean Δ R n,TOA is more positive under the high irrigation demand pathway (SSP3-7.0) than under SSP1-2.6, consistent with projected differences in irrigation expansion between scenarios. These results demonstrate that irrigation's radiative influence, while small in the global mean, is regionally substantial and scenario-dependent, with implications for the attribution of regional climate change and for the design of land-based mitigation trajectories.

articles.title: CFDID: a China Flood Disaster Impact Database from 1994 to 2023
articles.titleEn: CFDID: a China Flood Disaster Impact Database from 1994 to 2023
articles.abstract: China is one of the countries most severely affected by flood disasters. Long-term and systematic flood impact data are essential for flood risk assessment, flood impact model calibration, disaster prevention and reduction. However, an open, long-term, China-focused event-scale database with detailed flood disaster impact indicators remains lacking. Here we present the China Flood Disaster Impact Database (CFDID), which contains 1716 flood disaster event records from 1994 to 2023, including 1391 parent-event (L1) records. CFDID is compiled from 66 official documents and covers five flood-related disaster categories: rainstorm flood, typhoon, snowmelt flood, ice-jam flood, and dam-break flood. Each record includes date, location, disaster category, data source and available values for eight impact indicators: deaths and missing persons, affected population, affected cropland area, damaged cropland area, failed cropland area, collapsed dwellings, damaged dwellings, and direct economic losses. The database was constructed using a workflow that combines optical character recognition (OCR), large language model (LLM)-based information extraction, and manual verification, thereby improving the efficiency of converting unstructured text information into structured event records while ensuring data quality. Relative to the corresponding official national totals during 1994–2023, the impacts reported in L1 records in CFDID account for 68.49 % of deaths and missing persons, 72.24 % of affected population, 60.70 % of affected cropland area, 65.67 % of collapsed dwellings, and 74.86 % of direct economic losses. Compared with commonly used international flood impact databases, CFDID contains more detailed event records and accounts for higher percentages of the corresponding official totals for most impact indicators. CFDID also includes agricultural impact indicators, which are rarely available in international hazard impact databases. CFDID is available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22918521 (Cui et al., 2026) and will be continuously updated by year.

articles.title: Age of smoke sampled by aircraft during FIREX-AQ: methods and critical evaluation
articles.titleEn: Age of smoke sampled by aircraft during FIREX-AQ: methods and critical evaluation
articles.abstract: The age of smoke, meaning the time elapsed since it was produced in a fire, is an important parameter for interpreting measurements of evolving smoke composition. This study describes the smoke age estimates developed for large plumes sampled in the 2019 NASA-NOAA FIREX-AQ field experiment. Smoke ages are computed using two methods and applied to observations from two aircraft: the NASA DC-8 and NOAA Chemistry Twin Otter. The first method uses measurements of mean horizontal wind speed, as observed by the sampling aircraft, and distance to the fire to provide a single age estimate for each plume-crossing performed by the aircraft. While this “mean-wind method” uses accurate wind measurements, it can be systematically biased by assumptions that plume rise time is negligible and that winds are homogeneous horizontally and in time during the plume transport. Wind inhomogeneities due to terrain effects and day-to-night transition, among other factors, affected some plumes during FIREX-AQ. The mean-wind method therefore performs best for short-range transport over level terrain with steady winds. The second method relies on upwind air parcel trajectories and plume rise computed with multiple high-resolution meteorological datasets. This “trajectory-based method” quantifies age uncertainty from the meteorological ensemble, plume rise speed, wind speed errors, and fire location. The second method also resolves age differences from the center to edge of a transect. Still, it is susceptible to errors in the meteorological model. With careful comparison of the simulated trajectories to smoke transport observed from geostationary satellite imagery described here, we filter out many trajectory errors and improve the smoke age estimates. Across the two aircraft, the dataset provides ages for over 43 h (815 transects) of in situ measurements in smoke plumes from 115 different fires, with smoke ages ranging from 1 min to 40 h. The two age methods are strongly correlated ( R = 0.89) for the periods during FIREX-AQ when both ages are available. The mean-wind age is systematically 12 % younger than the trajectory-based age and the median absolute difference between them is 15 % (21 % for mean). The favorable agreement between the two age methods reflects that the mean-wind method was selectively applied to plumes with little wind variability. Trajectory-based ages are available for more of the FIREX-AQ smoke observations than the mean-wind ages. The median trajectory-based age uncertainty during FIREX-AQ is 24 % and the mean uncertainty is 37 %, due to a long-tailed distribution. The main source of age uncertainty is spread within the meteorological ensemble, followed by discrepancy between measured and modeled wind speed, then other factors like plume rise. The age uncertainty variable enables the user to identify periods with high or low confidence in the age estimate, thereby informing studies of smoke aging. Smoke ages data are available at https://doi.org/10.5067/ASDC/FIREXAQ_MetNav_ AircraftInSitu_DC8_Data_1 (Bennett et al., 2020) for the NASA DC-8 and https://doi.org/10.5067/ASDC/SUBORBITAL/ FIREXAQ_Analysis_N48_Data_1 (Holmes, 2021a) for the NOAA Chemistry Twin Otter.

articles.title: Compounding Human and Bioclimatic Factors Driving the Global Fire Crisis
articles.titleEn: Compounding Human and Bioclimatic Factors Driving the Global Fire Crisis
articles.abstract: Over millennia, social and ecological systems have been shaped by fire and have in turn shaped fire regimes. However, recent decades have seen an escalating “fire crisis” characterized by an increasing incidence of large, intense wildfires, most notably in forests. Voices in the academic literature and media often attribute the fire crisis to a narrow range of mechanisms, for example, fuel management or climate change. This failure to acknowledge the complexity of causes leads to simplistic framings of risk, and ultimately, proposed solutions that are either not feasible or may lead to undesired outcomes. In this review we outline the human and bioclimatic factors that are driving this fire crisis. Factors reviewed include the impacts of colonial legacies, which disrupted Indigenous land stewardship and traditional burning practices over centuries; policies of fire suppression; population growth, urbanization and land management practices; biotic disturbances such as insect outbreaks and invasive plant species; and climate change, which is affecting both fire regimes and social‐ecological resilience to fire. Many of these factors co‐occur leading to complex interactions and, often, unexpected outcomes. Our review highlights that climate change is now having a compounding effect, building on a multitude of other factors to drive the fire crisis. Addressing this crisis requires first acknowledging its complexity and moving beyond simple framings of risk. We suggest solutions will vary across different places and through time, but may include supporting Indigenous land stewardship, adopting flexible fire responses, shifting societal expectations from aggressive fire suppression to “living with fire”, and fostering resilient social and ecological communities.
