articles.title: Revealing the Widespread Bias of Extinction Risk in the Antarctic and the Southern Ocean
articles.titleEn: Revealing the Widespread Bias of Extinction Risk in the Antarctic and the Southern Ocean
articles.abstract: Accelerating environmental change in the Antarctic and Southern Ocean (ASO) necessitates robust extinction risk assessments to inform conservation priorities. Nevertheless, no systematic, region‐wide baseline of extinction risk currently exists for tracking ASO biodiversity responses to ongoing change, a significant barrier to global biodiversity monitoring. Here, we conducted the first ASO‐wide synthesis of current extinction risk knowledge for plants, animals and Fungi. This included examining biases in current assessments, the distribution of Threatened species and their associated threats. Using a data‐inclusive workflow, we compiled 8908 assessments representing 4970 species, more than doubling the number of ASO species assessed compared with any single source. As expected, assessments were heavily biased towards vertebrates (58% assessed), while invertebrates, despite their ecological prevalence, were markedly underrepresented (6% assessed). Among vertebrates, mammals had the highest proportion of Threatened species (26%). Birds within the ASO were disproportionately Threatened (25%) compared to the global average (11%), with the greatest threat for ASO species being ‘Biological Resource Use’. The sub‐Antarctic Islands had the highest density of both Threatened species and assessment effort, whereas many Antarctic species remain unassessed. Additionally, Threatened species have the lowest protected area coverage of any conservation status. These pronounced assessment biases highlight the need for more balanced, representative and data‐inclusive extinction risk assessments to be able to effectively detect conservation status change. This work represents an important step in ensuring ASO representation in global biodiversity monitoring frameworks, strengthening the capacity of these frameworks to detect, attribute and respond to future biodiversity changes.

articles.title: Towards improved integration of hydrological uncertainty and hydraulic model sensitivity in flood hazard mapping
articles.titleEn: Towards improved integration of hydrological uncertainty and hydraulic model sensitivity in flood hazard mapping
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The study presents a novel framework for integrating hydrological uncertainties and the related sensitivity of the hydrodynamic modelling results into flood hazard mapping. Uncertainties in flood frequency analysis (FFA), including anticipated impact of climate change and sensitivity to channel and floodplain roughness, were examined through selected scenario ensembles. The study area is the lower Vipava river, a transboundary catchment shared between Slovenia and Italy with variable floodplain topography. Sensitivity analysis revealed that uncertainty in FFA and river channel roughness significantly influenced the inundation spatial extent and inundation depth, the impact of floodplain roughness appears to be limited. The analysis shows that natural successional changes in river channel roughness substantially impact the results of a 10 year return period (RP) event, increasing flood extent by 45 %. The increase in inundated areas is less pronounced for 100 and 500 year RP floods, with increases of 15 % and 11 %, respectively. The weighted exceedance probability of inundation (WEPI) based on scenario ensembles provided an informative identification of areas most susceptible to potential changes in flood hazard. Our results highlight the value of targeted scenario ensembles that incorporate FFA uncertainty and hydraulic roughness sensitivity, thereby producing more informative flood hazard mapping that can complement deterministic mapping approaches and support more adaptive future land use planning.

articles.title: Composition, frequency, and severity of future rain-on-snow floods in Germany
articles.titleEn: Composition, frequency, and severity of future rain-on-snow floods in Germany
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: In Germany, severe widespread winter floods are often generated by rain-on-snow (ROS) phenomena. Under suitable conditions, when rain falls on the snow cover, the snow can melt and produce extreme amounts of runoff. In a warming climate, the frequency of ROS events is expected to change locally depending on elevation and regionally based on the general climate conditions. Consequently, the characteristics of ROS-driven winter floods are also anticipated to change. To investigate these changes, streamflow for multiple gauge stations in Germany was simulated using an ensemble of Long Short-Term Memory models based on an ensemble of downscaled climate projections. Germany, as a representative mid-latitude country with a considerable portion of historical floods generated by ROS, offers extensive spatial and temporal coverage of hydrological observations spanning long temporal scales, and hence warranting efficient training of the deep learning model. We used an explainable artificial intelligence method, integrated gradients, to examine flood-generating processes, focusing primarily on ROS, for every simulated flood peak. Changes in frequency, feature importance, and a ranking based severity of ROS flood events were assessed for individual streamflow gauges and for widespread floods affecting multiple catchments across four major river basins in Germany. We found that with regard to the ensemble median, the frequency of ROS floods will mostly decrease at the scale of individual gauges by up to 60 %, as well as at the widespread scale for the Rhine, Elbe, and Weser River basins but increase at gauges located in the Danube River basin for the corresponding widespread floods. For all regions, the snowmelt component during ROS floods becomes less relevant, whereas the contribution of rainfall to these events increases. Interestingly, the severity of the mean and the most extreme widespread ROS floods is projected to increase compared to the historical period in all major river basins in Germany. Only for individual gauges the severity may decrease in the future. Despite the overall agreement in the trends of the input features across climate models, the resulting trends in ROS floods are considerably disparate. This discrepancy is primarily attributed to complex model chains in the climate models leading to variability in rainfall and snowmelt, and to different melting seasons.

articles.title: From forecast to alert: an open-data AI flood early warning system with reservoir monitoring for the White Volta Basin
articles.titleEn: From forecast to alert: an open-data AI flood early warning system with reservoir monitoring for the White Volta Basin
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Flood early warning in the White Volta Basin of northern Ghana is complicated by unmonitored dam releases from Burkina Faso's Bagre Reservoir, which existing globally calibrated systems do not represent. We present an end-to-end AI-driven flood early warning system that integrates observed gauge discharge, CHIRPS satellite rainfall, ERA5-Land reanalysis forcing, and a novel JRC-derived Bagre reservoir storage proxy. An ensemble of Random Forest, XGBoost, and LSTM models trained on these inputs achieved Kling–Gupta Efficiency scores of 0.984, 0.974, and 0.957 at 1, 3, and 5 d lead times on an independent test period dominated by moderate flows (maximum 1206 m 3 s −1 , below the Orange alert threshold); higher-tier alert skill rests on leave-one-year-out cross-validation rather than held-out extreme events. Benchmarking against simple baselines shows the ensemble's advantage over a persistence forecast is marginal at 1 d lead but grows with lead time and concentrates on rising-limb and high-flow conditions, indicating that recent observed discharge carries most of the short-range skill while the ensemble's value lies at the longer horizons relevant to warning. For direct comparison, GloFAS v4 reanalysis discharge at Nawuni achieves KGE = −0.526 on the same test period, performing worse than a climatological mean predictor, primarily because LISFLOOD does not represent Bagre Dam release operations. A four-tier alert system calibrated to 30-year flood return periods achieved a cross-validated Red-tier probability of detection of 0.902 (false alarm ratio 0.134) at 1 d lead, declining to 0.762 at 5 d. Sentinel-1 SAR mapping provided spatial grounding for the discharge-based threshold framework, with Red-tier exceedance periods associated with floodplain inundation extents of 50 to 149 km 2 across three validation seasons. The system integrates into Ghana's existing myDEWETRA-VOLTALARM platform without requiring new institutional infrastructure. The Bagre reservoir proxy, derived from freely available JRC Global Surface Water imagery and validated against independent satellite altimetry ( r = 0.94), provides a measure of reservoir state. Because the reservoir fills to capacity in most wet seasons, this signal functions as an explicit model input and as seasonal situational awareness that the reservoir is capable of spilling, rather than as a standalone flood trigger.

articles.title: Comparing and validating modelled snow stability metrics
articles.titleEn: Comparing and validating modelled snow stability metrics
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: Recent developments in snow stability modelling demonstrated the great potential of numerical snow cover modelling for avalanche forecasting. These recently developed metrics provided promising results, possibly even superseding traditional stability indices. To further validate these results, we compared the temporal evolution of various stability metrics to a unique dataset of measurements, including snow stratigraphy, snow microstructure, and stability obtained at the high Alpine study site Steintälli above Davos (Eastern Swiss Alps) during the winter 2015/16. There, we measured the shear strength of a prominent weak layer of depth hoar crystals using the shear frame and assessed the propagation propensity of this weak layer with propagation saw tests. Concurrently, we characterized snow microstructure with the snow micro-penetrometer (SMP). At the study site, an automated weather station is located, providing the data to run the numerical snow cover model SNOWPACK so that modelled stability metrics can be derived. Field measurements showed that weak layer strength and toughness were initially low but increased over time, in parallel with the increasing slab load; all three parameters were correlated. While field observations focused on the most prominent weak layer, modelled stability metrics were evaluated for the persistent weak layers identified by the respective modelling approaches. These generally corresponded well to the layers visually identified in simulated snow stratigraphy. Data-driven and process-based stability metrics exhibited similar temporal evolution and comparable skill in relation to local avalanche activity, achieving overall accuracies of 53 %–68 %. This site-specific validation demonstrates that both types of numerical stability metrics provide valuable support for avalanche forecasting, although differences in their behaviour highlight the need for metric-specific interpretation. Hence, a multi-model approach may be advantageous for operational forecasting.

articles.title: Projection of the Status and Future Shifts of Topsoil Organic Carbon Stocks in Northern Hemisphere Permafrost Regions: Patterns and Drivers
articles.titleEn: Projection of the Status and Future Shifts of Topsoil Organic Carbon Stocks in Northern Hemisphere Permafrost Regions: Patterns and Drivers
articles.abstract: The Northern Hemisphere (NH) permafrost areas harbor vast reservoirs of soil organic carbon (SOC), which are potentially at serious releasing risk due to climate change. However, projections of future changes in SOC stocks in these regions remain subject to large uncertainties. In this study, we constructed an integrated approach that combines space‐for‐time substitution with a machine learning model to estimate the current status of surface (0–30 cm) SOC stocks in NH permafrost regions and to project their future changes throughout the 21st century under various Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSPs). The results indicate that approximately 224.2 Pg C were stored in NH permafrost regions during the baseline period (1981–2000), and they will remain relatively stable (−0.5% ± 0.9%) until the conclusion of 21st century under SSP1‐2.6, while a significant loss of about 8.5% ± 3.5% is projected under SSP5‐8.5. Spatially, the areas with increased surface SOC in the future are mainly located in the continuous permafrost zone, while the decrease is identified in most of discontinuous, sporadic, and isolated permafrost areas. Among ecosystems, grasslands and deserts are projected to act as future carbon sinks, while forests exhibit the largest declines. Temperature exerts the strongest control on SOC dynamics in the northern circumpolar (NC) permafrost region through a nonlinear threshold effect, whereas precipitation and vegetation productivity govern SOC changes in the Third Pole. These results highlight pronounced spatial heterogeneity of SOC dynamics in permafrost regions, providing valuable insights for carbon–climate feedback assessments and regional policy.

articles.title: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.titleEn: Tracing the spread of Celtic languages using ancient genomics
articles.abstract: Celtic languages are today restricted to Europe’s Atlantic fringes but were widely spoken across the continent during the Iron Age 1–3 . How Celtic achieved this early distribution remains contested 4 , with alternative archaeological and linguistic models proposing different homelands and dispersal routes. Here we analyse genome-wide data from 4,587 ancient individuals, focusing on Bronze and Iron Age Europe, to test the extent to which these models fit reconstructed demographic histories. We identify three main processes shaping European population structure that are relevant to the Celtic dispersal. First, the arrival of Steppe-related ancestry with Bell Beaker-associated groups after around 4400 bp (calibrated years before present or 1950 ce ) across the region in which Celtic and related languages were later spoken. Second, a movement from southwestern Europe into Britain during the Bronze Age (3800–3200 bp ), consistent with scenarios in which Celtic formed along the Atlantic façade. Third, a westward expansion of ancestry related to Late Bronze Age Knovíz–Urnfield-associated populations from eastern central Europe (3200–2800 bp ), affecting France, the British Isles, northeastern Iberia and Italy and later associated with Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène contexts 5–8 . Although all three movements have parallels with proposed models, we argue that the final movement, from eastern central Europe, is most parsimonious for the spread of Celtic. Although human history does not necessarily follow a parsimonious trajectory 9 and language shifts need not track genetic change, these results delimit the demographic scenarios that are plausible for the emergence of Celtic in prehistoric Europe.

articles.title: Continental water storage trends and budgets from the GRACE/GRACE-FO Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P)
articles.titleEn: Continental water storage trends and budgets from the GRACE/GRACE-FO Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P)
articles.abstract: The Global Gravity-based Groundwater Product (G3P) provides global groundwater storage (GWS) variations derived from GRACE/GRACE-FO terrestrial water storage (TWS) change by subtracting root-zone soil moisture, glacier mass change, surface water storage, and snow water equivalent. G3P thus provides the first globally consistent, publicly available groundwater dataset from satellite gravimetry for continental-scale water resources assessment. Here, we use G3P to assess global GWS trends over the extended GRACE/GRACE-FO record, jointly with TWS and the subtracted storage components. A central challenge is that apparent long-term trends in GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage records can reflect persistent storage change, natural climate variability, hydrological memory, and observational errors, complicating trend detection and continental-scale storage-change budgets. We address this using a calibrated trend-analysis framework that jointly accounts for trend, seasonal, and stochastic variations in each grid-cell time series. Statistically significant trends are then aggregated to quantify volumetric GWS and TWS gains, losses, and net changes at continental and global scales. Applying this framework to 21.5 years of data (April 2002–September 2023), we find that groundwater depletion is a major contributor to freshwater decline at continental scales, most prominently in Asia (−55 km 3 yr −1 ), while cryospheric mass loss dominates the strongest TWS declines in high-latitude and glacierized regions. Pronounced regional contrasts include increasing groundwater storage across large parts of Africa (+37 km 3 yr −1 ), negative trends in drought-affected regions, and widespread negative or near-threshold GWS tendencies across the Northern Hemisphere. Globally, significance-filtered net GWS and TWS changes are approximately −27 and −183 km 3 yr −1 , respectively. The corresponding gross negative GWS change of approximately 103 km 3 yr −1 is of the same order as model-based estimates of global groundwater depletion. Sensitivity tests indicate robust results: at 95 %, detected area increases by 30 % for TWS and 36 % for GWS, while net-loss magnitudes rise by only 9 % and 18 %. Across much of the seasonal-to-interannual spectral range, GWS is the dominant individual storage-component signal within TWS, which highlights the importance of groundwater for continental freshwater availability.

articles.title: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
articles.titleEn: Unreported mass movement cascades and future Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) hazard in Jammu and Kashmir, Western Himalaya
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The Warwan sub-basin in Jammu and Kashmir is a remote glaciated region containing several glacial lakes and has recently experienced population growth and infrastructure development. Due to inaccessibility and geomorphic masking, multiple mass movement events, including avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs), have remained largely unreported. This study analyzes three major avalanche events from the past two decades. articles.title: Integration of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions With a Land‐Atmosphere Coupled Model in the Gray Zone
articles.titleEn: Integration of Aerosol–Cloud Interactions With a Land‐Atmosphere Coupled Model in the Gray Zone
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Clouds strongly impact net surface radiation, creating differential heating patterns, and trigger land breezes that in turn organize cloud development. These dial processes determine the location of persistent ecohydrological regimes at local scales. Aerosol–cloud interactions (ACI) directly impact the diurnal cycle of cloud optical depth, and therefore the surface energy budget; yet they are generally not explicitly represented in studies of land‐atmosphere interactions. To address this gap, a 3D Large‐Eddy Simulation model was modified to describe ACI in the gray zone. The goal is to simulate realistic cumulus cloud dynamics consistent with the spatial dynamics of land surface moisture and temperature, and associated boundary layer processes. The model is tested and evaluated using simulations at hectometer resolution with prescribed diurnal surface heating corresponding to idealized wet (low Bowen ratio [LBR]) and dry (high Bowen ratio [HBR]) surface boundary conditions. Expected cloud sensitivity is well captured: compared to LBR, HBR clouds have a significantly higher cloud base (about 1 km), up to 50% reduction in total cloud fraction, and cloudiness ends earlier by about 2 hr due to enhanced turbulence and lower moisture availability. Analyses of the evolution of 3D cloud drop size distributions show that the model captures the cloud life cycle, including aerosol activation, condensational growth, enhanced collision‐coalescence, and aerosol regeneration. The results show that resolved eddy‐scale (sub‐km) within‐cloud circulations modulate cloud microphysical structure by locally altering supersaturation at minute timescales. Successive aerosol regeneration yields coarser cloud condensation nuclei, producing a coarse‐aerosol mode, and impacting mid‐day cloud fraction and cloudiness persistence.

articles.title: Advancing Satellite Solar‐Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence Data Assimilation in Land Surface Models: An Assessment Over Boreal Evergreen Needleleaf Forests
articles.titleEn: Advancing Satellite Solar‐Induced Chlorophyll Fluorescence Data Assimilation in Land Surface Models: An Assessment Over Boreal Evergreen Needleleaf Forests
articles.journal: Journal of Advances in Modeling Earth Systems
articles.abstract: Boreal forests represent about 20% of the global forest carbon sink and contribute to climate change mitigation, yet land surface models (LSMs) struggle to simulate their gross primary production (GPP). Space‐borne observations of solar‐induced fluorescence (SIF) have been used to improve LSM GPP through data assimilation. However, previous work has shown that assimilating SIF alone can degrade GPP for some vegetation types, highlighting the need for enhanced process representation and tightly constrained parameters. Uncertainties in the representation of non‐photochemical quenching (NPQ), which regulates the SIF‐GPP relationship, further complicate this challenge. Here, we develop a data assimilation strategy to assess the complementarity of satellite SIF from TROPOMI and in situ GPP in constraining GPP dynamics simulated by the ORCHIDEE LSM over boreal evergreen needleleaf forests. We evaluate this framework using two NPQ schemes, a process‐based formulation separating sustained and reversible components, and a generic model representing total NPQ. After assimilation, evaluation against independent SIF grid cells and flux sites shows improved seasonal cycles of both SIF and GPP. Regional‐scale simulations better match independent GPP products (FLUXSAT and FLUXCOM‐X‐BASE) over 2001–2020, with over 77% RMSD reduction in the mean seasonal cycle versus the prior, largely reflecting the recalibration of model parameters after implementation of the new radiative transfer scheme. SIF‐GPP co‐assimilation outperforms GPP‐only assimilation for the GPP latitudinal profile, and also for the GPP mean seasonal cycle in three out of four cases. Although the two NPQ models affect the simulated SIF seasonal cycle differently, their performances after assimilation are similar.

articles.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
articles.titleEn: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
articles.abstract: When anthropogenic CO 2 emissions cease, global temperature does not stabilize immediately. The resulting global temperature change, the zero emissions commitment, is central to carbon budget assessments and understanding reversibility of global warming, yet its dependence on prior warming levels remains unclear. Here we show, using zero-emission simulations with the UK Earth System Model (UKESM1.2) across global warming levels of 1.5–5 K, that the zero emissions commitment stays near zero up to 2 K but becomes positive at higher warming levels, reaching 0.4–0.6 K after ~ 150 years. This dependence indicates that stabilizing or reversing warming becomes progressively more difficult as peak temperature rises. We identify the mechanism behind this behaviour: stronger warming from higher radiative disequilibrium and weakening carbon sinks, driven by saturated land carbon uptake and the reduced radiative impact of CO 2 drawdown at higher background CO 2 concentrations. Higher peak warming therefore commits the planet to additional warming, limiting temperature-overshoot reversibility.

articles.title: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.titleEn: Global-scale meteorological-to-groundwater drought propagation and the drivers and patterns of multi-year groundwater drought
articles.abstract: Groundwater stores a third of all global freshwater and supports water supply, irrigation and ecosystems across the world. As such, groundwater drought can have wide-reaching financial, social and environmental impacts, particularly when drought events are prolonged or multi-year. Although recent work has made significant progress in understanding the drivers and patterns of multi-year meteorological droughts, we do not know how this signal translates into multi-year groundwater drought, where subsurface processes, anthropogenic influences and abstractions can alter the meteorological signal. This is particularly true at the global-scale, where a major barrier to understanding large-scale groundwater drought dynamics is the difficulty of obtaining consistent and comprehensive groundwater data. In this research, we use a new global hyper-resolution (∼1 km) groundwater dataset to investigate the global patterns and drivers of groundwater drought from 1960–2019, with a specific focus on multi-year events. We start by characterizing the propagation of meteorological (represented by SPEI-12) to groundwater drought, evaluating how and to what extent the sub-surface plays a role in modulating the meteorological drought signal. Subsequently, we define three global groundwater response types that provide a framework for understanding the processes and geo-physical drivers of normal versus multi-year groundwater droughts. We find that 35 % of global groundwater grid cells have an average groundwater drought duration which is multi-year. In 83 % of these locations, the subsurface extends the meteorological drought signal, whereas in the remaining 17 %, groundwater drought duration appears to be primarily driven by meteorological anomalies. Our analysis offers new insights into global-scale drought exposure by identifying regions which have been most vulnerable to multi-year groundwater drought in the past, as well as those which might be more vulnerable in the future. Importantly, our typology also highlights areas where multi-year groundwater droughts can be anticipated based on meteorological drought anomalies and can therefore inform strategies for managing and mitigating future water scarcity risks.

articles.title: Monthly-updated territorial fossil CO 2 emissions estimates for Japan
articles.titleEn: Monthly-updated territorial fossil CO 2 emissions estimates for Japan
articles.abstract: We present a low-lag, monthly dataset of emissions of carbon dioxide from fossil fuel consumption and industrial processes in Japan, derived directly from official activity data and starting in 2007. Such estimates will be crucial for near-real-time monitoring of emissions and making swift policy responses accordingly. When aggregated, our estimates replicate the annual data published through the UNFCCC national inventory report very well, with only small discrepancies which we describe and quantify. The dataset is produced with a lag of 2 months and can be used to estimate the annual emissions a year ahead of the official estimates submitted to the UNFCCC, and also provides a better starting point for short-term emissions projections. Data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20023226 (Kunimitsu and Andrew, 2026).

articles.title: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.titleEn: Field surveying and numerical simulation of the Typhoon Hato storm surge event in Guangdong province, China
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: In 2017, Typhoon Hato hitting Zhuhai city, Guangdong province, caused a severe storm surge disaster. In this study, a systematic field survey of the “Hato” storm surge was conducted and the numerical modeling of inundation extent and depth was performed. The survey integrated floating debris tracking, inundation tracing, and local inquiries to determine the seawater inundation edge points, water depths, and overall extent of the flooding. Combined with field reconnaissance, the mechanisms damaging typical hazard-bearing bodies during marine disasters were clarified, and the effects of the “Hato” storm surge were analyzed. Inundated areas were distributed in coastal cities, with the maximum inundation depth up to about 2 m, and the inundated area exceeding 54.08 km 2 . Compared to historical storm surge records, Typhoon Hato ranked as the fourth most severe and stands as one of the most devastating storm surges to impact Guangdong province over the past decade. In addition, the proposed model can reproduce this typhoon and storm surge event, which was evaluated by comparing field observations with numerical simulations, showing good consistency with the observed flooding records. These results could provide detailed data and decision support, which can be used as guidance for the mitigation of future storm surges in coastal areas.

articles.title: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.titleEn: Persistence of scour at bridges using stochastic simulations
articles.journal: Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences
articles.abstract: The stochastic and deterministic properties of the scouring process at bridges are analysed by coupling synthetic streamflow generations with a scour and fill model considering the upstream sediment supply. Streamflow was generated using the asymmetric moving-average (AMA) scheme that preserves the Hurst-Kolmogorov (HK) dynamics, the second-order dependence structure, time asymmetry, and the first four statistical moments of the marginal distribution. Stationarity, homogeneity, and ergodicity of the streamflow and scouring processes were assumed. Monte Carlo analyses covered 12 000 realisations for each of the three considered scenarios with different upstream sediment supply. Extreme scour events were assessed using annual maxima with GEV fitting and compared against the equilibrium scour. The dependence structure was identified with the climacogram and climacospectrum stochastic tools and fitted with a filtered HK model (FHK-CD). The obtained results show a multi-scale dynamics of the scouring process with rough and weak persistent behaviour ( M ≈0.40; H ≈0.60), while envelopes span from antipersistent to strongly persistent scour regimes ( H up to ≈0.86) depending on the upstream sediment supply. It is worth noting that the upstream sediment supply reduced the envelope variability and modified the extreme scour values. Additionally, synchronisation between extreme events of streamflow and scour showed a weak correspondence (Critical Success Index ≈0.15–0.60), indicating that streamflow extremes do not systematically translate into scour extremes. Finally, scour depths with a given return period (computed from scour time series) increase with upstream sediment supply.

articles.title: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Evaluation of snow water equivalent from large-scale land-surface products over Italy
articles.abstract: Snow water equivalent (SWE) is a critical hydrological variable for water resource management in mountainous regions, where seasonal snowpacks function as natural reservoirs regulating streamflow and water supply. While high-resolution, observation-constrained regional or national snow products provide reliable daily SWE estimates at fine spatial resolution (less than 1 km), their limited temporal coverage often restricts their use for long-term hydro-climatological studies. Large-scale land-surface products, in which SWE is derived from land-surface model simulations driven by atmospheric reanalyses or regional dynamical downscaling systems, provide multi-decadal coverage, but their reliability may be affected by biases in meteorological forcing, limited topographic representation, and simplified snow process parameterisation, requiring rigorous regional evaluation. This study evaluates the SWE estimates of three large-scale land-surface products, i.e., the global ERA5-Land, the European CERRA-Land, and the Italian VHR-REA_IT, against the national reference dataset IT-SNOW across Italy. The analysis combines grid-scale bias assessment of mean annual SWE and snow cover duration with temporal correlation analysis of daily SWE series, and is complemented by an evaluation of precipitation and temperature biases in each product, providing insight into how each product represents the atmospheric conditions governing snow accumulation and ablation and thereby supporting the interpretation of the identified SWE discrepancies. The results show clear regional differences in product performance, with no single product performing best across all metrics. ERA5-Land shows the strongest temporal correlation with IT-SNOW, but tends to overestimate mean annual SWE and snow cover duration in the Alps. CERRA-Land shows more moderate biases than ERA5-Land in the Italian Alps, but generally underestimates mean annual SWE across most subregions, where autumn and winter precipitation deficits in the forcing limit snow accumulation. Across the Apennines, both ERA5-Land and CERRA-Land tend to underestimate SWE and snow cover duration, particularly in the northern sectors. VHR-REA_IT shows widespread underestimation and the weakest temporal correspondence with IT-SNOW despite its finer grid spacing, which may be due to its fully coupled atmosphere–land architecture with no assimilation of meteorological observations. Overall, the results suggest that forcing biases explain a substantial part of the observed SWE discrepancies, although not all of them. This study provides useful insights for the use of SWE estimates from large-scale land-surface products in long-term hydro-climatological assessments over Italy and helps to understand whether the products can be used to evaluate snow dynamics in mountainous regions lacking high-quality benchmark estimates.

articles.title: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.titleEn: Technical note: Benefits of Bayesian estimation of model parameters in a large hydrological model ensemble
articles.abstract: Quantifying and mitigating parametric and structural uncertainties in hydrological models are crucial to accurately understand and predict the rainfall-runoff process. Despite recent advances in Bayesian approaches for quantifying structural uncertainty using very large hydrological model ensembles, the simultaneous quantification of both parametric and structural uncertainties has yet to be implemented since previous works on large model ensembles have relied on deterministic optimization of parameters. Here we present the potential benefits of Bayesian estimation of parametric uncertainty within a large hydrological model ensemble. We find that Bayesian estimation of model parameters (more generally, change in calibration methods) potentially influences the interpretation of model comparisons. Specifically, Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification greatly benefits complex models with many parameters, thereby affecting discussions of the appropriate level of model complexity. We also find that Bayesian parametric uncertainty quantification does not substantially improve multi-model hydrological predictions. The adverse effects of parameter misspecification in individual models are effectively mitigated by combining models with diverse structures. Thus, the high computational cost of Bayesian parameter estimation is not paid for to improve rainfall-runoff analysis in a large hydrological model ensemble.

articles.title: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.titleEn: Global socio-economic resilience to disasters
articles.abstract: Most disaster risk assessments use asset damages as their central metric, often neglecting distributional impacts and affected people’s coping and recovery capacity. To address this, the concepts of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience—the ability to experience asset damages without a decline in well-being—have been proposed. Here we provide a global picture of well-being losses and socio-economic resilience using microsimulations. Across 132 countries, 1 dollar in damages causes well-being losses equivalent to a 2-dollar uniform national consumption drop. The poorest populations incur only 9% of damages but 33% of well-being losses. A 10% higher gross domestic product per capita is associated with a 1 percentage point resilience increase. Low-income countries experience 72% greater well-being losses per dollar of damages and need 92% longer to recover than high-income countries. Socio-economic and financial interventions can complement asset-focused policies, and targeting low-income populations usually yields higher well-being returns. Our results offer a starting point for a discussion on more comprehensive risk metrics and risk management policies for sustainable development.

articles.title: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.titleEn: Vegetation increasingly controlled by atmospheric dryness rather than soil moisture
articles.abstract: Terrestrial vegetation regulates global carbon cycling and climate through responses to water availability. Yet, it remains unclear whether soil moisture (SM) or atmospheric dryness (vapour pressure deficit, VPD) dominates vegetation responses and, more critically, how their relative influence changes over time, limiting predictions of ecosystem–climate feedback under warming. Here we analyse satellite-derived vegetation variability over the past four decades using an explainable artificial intelligence framework that disentangles nonlinear hydroclimatic driver contributions. We show SM dominates vegetation variability in most regions. However, VPD influence has strengthened while SM influence has weakened over time. These changes highlight an asymmetric transition with more SM-dominated ecosystems shifting towards increasing VPD control than vice versa. Changes in the mean and variability of SM and VPD drive this transition by altering plant water-stress responses. Continued warming will probably intensify this pattern as rising VPD and more frequent extreme events strengthen atmospheric constraints on vegetation.

articles.title: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.titleEn: On combining climate models into weighted ensembles
articles.abstract: Several methods have been proposed and used to refine estimates of future climate change based on combined output from comprehensive climate models. While previously the so-called model democracy approach was used to combine model outputs, where every model is given equal weight, it is now widely accepted that using model weights that account for model performance and model independence is necessary to obtain more reliable results. However, most existing approaches rely, implicitly or explicitly, on a similar statistical basis, while describing things in different ways. Here we distinguish between approaches that are based on the performance of individual models (individual performance weighting) and approaches that are based on the performance of the weighted ensemble as a whole (ensemble performance weighting). At the same time, we formulate both in probabilistic Bayesian terms to make their application and comparison straightforward. Using simple constructed examples, we demonstrate that the ensemble performance weighting approach implicitly accounts for co-dependencies among models, which arguably makes the computation of independence weights for the purpose of model weighting obsolete. We also show that a set of weighted models within the ensemble weighting approach will naturally tend to artificially reduce uncertainty and that this is strongly influenced by the choice of the prior distribution over weight vectors. The distinction between individual and ensemble performance weighting is both methodological and conceptual. Formulating both approaches in general probabilistic Bayesian terms as done here, can serve as a common basis for future developments with regard to ensemble model weighting in Earth system science. The discussed concepts are generally applicable across domains and are thus possibly relevant for other modeling communities as well.

articles.title: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.titleEn: Unexpected land-surface warming following a relatively limited-forcing hypothetical nuclear war
articles.abstract: Nuclear conflicts could ignite intense fires that inject considerable amounts of black carbon (BC) into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, with the potential to disrupt global climate. While uncertainties in the BC injection remain large, relatively few modeling studies have explored the climatic response to more limited nuclear exchange between major nuclear powers. Here, we investigate the climate response to a set of relatively limited-forcing scenarios (12 to 24 Tg BC) for nuclear exchanges between the United States and Russia. This corresponds to one-tenth to one-fifth of the forcing strength of typically considered. We use the Canadian Earth System Model version 5, an independent contributor to the worldwide set of Earth System Models that has not been explored previously in this application. Consistent with previous work, decreased downwelling shortwave radiation at the surface drives prolonged surface cooling. Unexpectedly, however, a transient surface warming develops in the first boreal summer following a boreal-winter injection, linked to reduced cooling via net longwave and turbulent fluxes. The transient warming is most pronounced for the lowest forcing cases. Precipitation, which decreases even while the surface warms, is found to be controlled by stabilizing, top-heavy warming. Multi-model assessment of these relatively limited-forcing cases is warranted given their potential impacts.

articles.title: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.titleEn: Benchmarking conditioners in Liang–Kleeman Information Flow: application to land–atmosphere interactions in humid forests
articles.abstract: The Liang–Kleeman Information Flow (LKIF) framework has been increasingly used to identify causality in Earth–system dynamics in recent years. Yet, uncertainties remain regarding how the causal graph changes when mediators and confounders (conditioners) are introduced, i.e., divergence between the bivariate and conditioned forms. A controlled synthetic experiment shows that LKIF preserves correct causal directions under hidden confounding, while differences between bivariate and multivariate estimates still occur. We characterize these differences using time-varying LKIF and introduce several quantifiers, including Conditioner Dominance Index, Moderation Gain, Conditioning Pressure, and Convergence Rate, to evaluate the contributions of conditioners. This is illustrated in an application to soil moisture (SM) and vapor pressure deficit (VPD) couplings with vegetation (leaf area index (LAI) and gross primary productivity (GPP)) in humid forest regions of Southeast China and the Amazon Basin, using satellite-derived and reanalysis data over 1981–2018. We find that the influence of SM on LAI remains consistently stable and shows little sensitivity to the selected conditioners, whereas its influence on GPP and that of VPD on vegetation exhibit substantial divergence between bivariate and multivariate estimates. This divergence peaks under compound dry–hot conditions, with VPD and temperature emerging as dominant conditioners. These results demonstrate that bivariate and multivariate LKIF can yield markedly different conclusions across time and space, especially under compound environmental stress. More importantly, even for the same variables in a causal graph, the same conditioners can affect the temporal evolution of the causal relationships very differently at different locations. This highlights how stationary assumptions may oversimplify causal structure by masking relevant temporal transitions, particularly under compound environmental stress.

articles.title: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.titleEn: From paper to proof: revealing Congo Basin warming through rescued climate archives
articles.abstract: The Congo Basin in Central Africa remains one of the few regions globally where the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has neither assessed changes in hot extremes and extreme precipitation since the 1950s nor attributed such changes to anthropogenic influences, primarily due to the sparsity of in situ observational data. Although extensive daily weather records exist, spanning from the 1900s to the early 2000s and covering numerous stations across the basin, the majority of these remain archived on paper, limiting their accessibility for climate analysis. Here we present and analyse over 1 million temperature and precipitation observations from 37 weather stations in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, which have until now been unavailable to the research community. To produce this dataset, we first digitized (imaged) 9885 paper sheets stored in local archives during two dedicated field campaigns. We subsequently apply an improved version of the MeteoSaver software (version 1.1) to transcribe the imaged sheets, yielding daily time series of maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, precipitation, as well as dry bulb and wet bulb temperatures measured at three times per day (06:00, 15:00, and 18:00 local time). After quality control, analysis of multi-decadal temperature data across the basin reveals a consistent and accelerating warming signal since the 1960s, characterized by a warming shift in the distribution of daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures with each successive decade. Median trends across 21 of the 37 stations with sufficient data availability are 0.22, 0.10, and 0.15 °C per decade for daily maximum, minimum, and average temperatures, respectively, corresponding to approximately 0.7, 0.3, and 0.5 °C of warming during the 1961–1990 period. We further find an increasing frequency of hot extremes and a decreasing frequency of cold extremes with each successive decade, with the most recent decade exhibiting nearly twice as many hot days per year and fewer cold days compared to the earliest decade. Analysis of precipitation at three stations with sufficient data indicates an increased frequency of heavy precipitation events at two stations and no substantial change at the third; however, limited spatial coverage due to data availability restricts broader conclusions for the DRC. Overall, this analysis of rescued weather data from Central Africa highlights the urgent need to close the knowledge gap on climate trends in the Congo Basin, one of the world's most data-sparse yet climatically significant regions.

articles.title: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.titleEn: Can we define climate by means of an ensemble? A tale of time scales of convergence
articles.abstract: It is not really questioned today that climate can be described in theory by an ensemble of trajectories differing in their initial conditions, which is then translated to numerical ensembles in climate models. It is also widely accepted that any evolution observed within a few decades after initialization is not yet relevant to climate. Evolution at a later stage, instead, is then used to characterize climate and its change, under the implicit assumption that slower processes do not considerably contribute to differences between ensemble members, allowing internal variability of climate to be identified with these differences. However, a careful justification for this practice is as yet lacking. In particular, a definition of climate in support of this practice is outstanding, including the identification of the kind of time scales at play through providing an argumentation for their relevance. Our study aims at filling this gap. After pointing out that the most important criterion for a definition of climate is the uniqueness of the probability measure on which the definition relies, we first recall the naive proposal to represent such a probability measure by the distribution of ensemble members that has, loosely speaking, converged to the natural probability measure of the so-called snapshot or pullback attractor of the dynamics. We then consider the time scales of convergence and refine the proposal by taking a probability measure that is conditional on the (possibly time-evolving) state of modes characterized by convergence time scales longer than the horizon of a particular study. We design an ensemble simulation initialization scheme for studying convergence time scales and uniqueness of ensembles in Earth system models.

articles.title: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.titleEn: Impacts of simulated coastal ocean alkalinity enhancement on the seasonal carbon cycle in European waters under a low- and a high-emission scenario
articles.abstract: One potentially scalable method to remove CO 2 from the air is ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE), which works to lower the ocean's CO 2 partial pressure ( p CO 2 ) and accelerate CO 2 sequestration and durable storage. This study explores how OAE might affect the seasonal carbon cycle, which plays a key role in the ocean's annual CO 2 uptake. By analysing Earth System Model simulations of OAE implemented continuously at the European coastline under low and high emissions, it was found that: (a) due to surface alkalinity retention, OAE reduces ocean p CO 2 most strongly in summer, turning the region into a year-round carbon sink; (b) the strongest air-sea CO 2 uptake enhancement takes place in winter; (c) the ocean's carbon sink is increased more strongly in SSP3-7.0 than in SSP1-2.6 due to a lower buffering capacity.

articles.title: Decoded Antarctic snow accumulation history reconciles observed and modeled trends in accumulation and large-scale warming patterns
articles.titleEn: Decoded Antarctic snow accumulation history reconciles observed and modeled trends in accumulation and large-scale warming patterns
articles.abstract: Increased snow accumulation on the Antarctic Ice Sheet mitigated global sea level rise by ∼ 11 mm during 1901–2000 according to ice core reconstructions. However, in the most recent 40 years of more intense observation and warming, the trend in the Antarctic-wide accumulation rate has been negligible. We attribute these trends by evaluating Earth system model experiments in comparison with dynamically consistent reconstructions of surface climate. Single-forcing experiments reveal that rising concentrations of greenhouse gases (GHGs) have been the underlying driver of increased accumulation, yet acting alone would have caused twice the observed accumulation-related sea level mitigation during 1901–2000. Aerosol-driven cooling partially compensates this overprediction, but the reconstructions provide evidence that poorly modeled processes can explain observation-model trend discrepancies. In particular, these data support a hypothesis that high-latitude winds have been working together with ice-shelf meltwater fluxes to dampen Southern Ocean surface warming and suppress the GHG-driven accumulation increase since the initiation of West Antarctic ice shelf thinning in the mid-20th Century. The wind pattern associated with strengthening of the Southern Hemisphere westerlies and deepening of the Amundsen Sea Low distributes accumulation unevenly across the continent in an orographic pattern that is consistent across models and the reconstructions. In reconstructions, these same wind and accumulation patterns are associated with muted surface warming across the eastern Pacific and Southern Ocean, a pattern not captured in climate projections including the all-forcings large ensemble studied here. However, the westerly wind history constrained by paleoclimate data assimilation largely reconciles differences between the model's ensemble-mean response and the observed world for both Antarctic-wide accumulation and large-scale warming patterns. Although the large ensemble simulates similar wind histories to the real one – driven by internal variability and anthropogenic forcing – its corresponding responses in SSTs and Antarctic-wide snow accumulation are decoupled from the wind. We discuss how this significant observation-model discrepancy, which has implications for projecting regional climate change, likely arises from omitted meltwater forcing and/or resolution limitations. As a component of the sea level budget and a gauge of the magnitude and spatial pattern of climate change, Antarctic snow accumulation is a critical target for models to replicate.
